title: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
text: Just beat the game and i must say its a very nice story driven little "Game". Calling it a game is a bit wrong since this is mostly "just" a Choose your own adventure type game, with few elements that actually require thinking. I enjoyed it and played through it in one sitting. Its a bit sad that they dont have any voiceactors that would have given this game considerably more depth. As it stands i didnt regret my decision to buy it. The Story revolves around you working basically for the ingame NSA, except that ingame the NSA has considerably less resources at its desposal. You are tasked in investigating a Terrorist Bombing. You do that by going with a finely toothed comb through the lives of the people who may be of interest. You learn they likes, their dislikes. They sexual Orientation, Their Friends and foes, Their Medical history and so much more. This game manages to show how much of a total strangers life can be found just by the things they say publically. Thought provoking game indeed. Sadly its not much of a game, but i dont regret spending money on it. Btw i beat the game in one sitting, so its not overly long but as i said i dont regret it, but its a YMMV type situation.

title: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
text: I had pretty good idea of what to expect when I started playing Orwell, but I was surprised time and time again about the absolutely amazing writing and the whole premise of the game. While not being overly complex in its mechanics, Orwell provides an emotional experience like few other games I have ever played and is able to capture the dystopian vibe of 1984 to an extremely disturbing level. I started my first playthrough in the evening and it gripped me so much that I couldn't stop playing until I had finished the game some time around 3 a.m. While the game doesn't offer a lot of choices, most of these actually do matter and then fold out in a logical way. Contrary to telltale games, choices have an actual emotional impact on the player, which is something I haven't seen often in videogaming. Everyone even remotely interested in storytelling and the workings of society should have played this to completion at least once. Especially people who think they have nothing to hide and don't see an issue with the paradigm of security above all. This game does actually successfully deliver a very disturbing perspective.

title: Osmos
text: Osmos is based around a fairly simple concept. You are a mote. You propel yourself by shooting out part of your own mass. You get absorbed by motes larger than you. You absorb motes smaller than you. On every level, you are attempting to grow much larger. There is a time control mechanism allowing you to speed up and slow down how quickly time passes. This is essential. Why you may need to speed up time: You're moving in the correct direction, but very slowly. You could speed yourself up by shooting out more of your mass, but you generally don't want to waste mass doing that. Why you may need to slow down time:  Sometimes things are moving fast and you need to propel yourself in a very particular direction. Pros + Decent variety of levels. For example: * Entire map covered with motes and the motes are non-moving. You start in middle and have to carefully maneuver yourself around. Be careful! The pieces you shoot out can hit the other motes and start to move them. These feel a little bit like puzzles. * Orbits. You and other motes orbit around one or more "Attractor" motes. * Sentient motes. You have to absorb some motes that have some basic AI. + The orbit prediction arc. This arc predicts your orbit around another object.  You can then see if your path matches what you want. The game would've been too hard without it. Cons - Can be very frustrating. You may have been playing a level for 10-15 minutes when you lose because of: * a moment of inattention. * you realize you've reached an unwinnable state. That one other mote you need to absorb is just a tiny bit bigger than you.  (Note: the game will warn you when the level has reached an unwinnable state. You'll see "Doesn't look good..." at the bottom of the screen. However, that warning is often late.) Overall If you're prepared for a lot of frustration, Osmos can be a rewarding game.

text: I rate Osmos 4/5. Good... ...but this game can quickly become frustrating and is extremely difficult. Indeed, I remember an old "friendlyware" dos-based lunar lander game I had which sought to have fairly realistic controls. This is harder than that game ever was. In this game you control some sort of microscopic super-organism (I always pretend it's some sort of genetically engineered thing) and generally try to make it become the biggest creature in the petri dish (or microscope slide rather). You control it by ejecting parts of itself out in particular directions. Hence moving makes you smaller. You consume any other creatures (well most other creatures) which are also smaller than you are (bump into them to consume them) to get bigger (In a way it reminds me of that old Mortal Engines young adult book except there it was entire cities, not micro-organisms). The bigger you are the more you need to eject to move or even change direction. This dynamic quickly gets really complicated and challenging because you have to balance your need to move (both to hunt and to avoid danger) with your need to consume. I admit the game is now too hard for me to win (I'd have to be totally obsessed with this game to even try at this point) but despite this I still had a lot of fun getting to this point along the way. This game has peaceful, relaxing music and has a great visual athstetic. This is certainly one of the best, though one of the hardest, puzzle games I have ever played.

title: Overgrowth
text: I liked Lugaru. So much so, that I think it's in my top 10 games of all time, despite being so short. Naturally I really wanted to like this one too. It's basically Lugaru 2 with great animations, physics and modern graphics, after all. However it's not only unfinished even after a decade of development, but it's just simply not as good as Lugaru, it's predecessor from 2005. It is really ruined not by it's unfinished state, but by bad design choices and a seeming lack of understanding of risk and reward and overall combat mechanics. Which is baffling, seeing how great and balanced those very mechanics were in Lugaru. It's almost like the original developer of Lugaru didn't have any voice in the desing of Overgrowth, and the new designers didn't learn anything from Lugaru. In Lugaru the bunnykick was a high risk - high reward move. In Overgrowth there is almost no risk to it and it is so powerful that it doesn't actually make sense to use any other move in the game. The best way to fight is to not fight at all, and instead repeatedly jump over the enemies bunnykicking them. Also the dodge in the game is useless, since you can just jump away from attacks. Unlike in Lugaru, the enemy doesn't pull you back to the ground if you try to jump too close to them. Even if you get trapped in the middle of 4 armed enemies, you can just jump away as if nothing happened. Even if the jump wasn't stupidly overpowered, the dodge should still be integrated in to the block. Simply make it so that if you succesfully block an attack that cannot be blocked, Turner dodges instead, and not have dodge and block be 2 separate actions. That's just unnecessary complexity that doesn't add anything to the game. Also for some reason succesfully blocking an attack no longer does a counter that can then be then countered again. Instead it just blocks, unless you hold the block key after the block. Why can't he just finish the move without the player having to hold the key? And the button-hold-counter isn't even a counter anymore, it's just a judo throw. Which doesn't make sense since countering a rather quick animation in a short time window is something you should be rewarded for. Instead of anticipating the enemy and utilizing counterattacks, often the best way to win a fight, apart from the bunnykick, is to just spam attack. If you have a knife, all you have to do is run backwards and hold attack and Turner will slash the pursuing enemy to death while they do nothing but run in knife range. In lugaru you couldn't attack enemies running behind you unless you stopped to meet them. Wolf attacks cannot be blocked at all, so the only viable way to beat them now is to spam the new OP bunnykick on them, which removes any actual challenge from the toughest enemy in the game, as it does from everything else. Also legsweep, is almost useless now, and punches are so quick that it's almost impossible to react to them. Weapons almost never get disarmed with a counter attack, and instead most often get thrown away from the user only when he gets smashed to the gound. There are a plethora of mostly useless and a few overpowered attacks, instead of the few and all around useful and well balanced attacks in Lugaru. There were a few positive changes made to the gameplay as well. Not enough to compensate for the bad and broken ones, but still. The increased stealth speed is nice. It bothered me in Lugaru how you had to be constantly rolling if you ever wanted to actually reach someone unnoticed. The removal of the need to be crouching in order to jump higher is also good, since it removes unnecessary complexity in the controls Most of the time in Lugaru I didn't even remember that I could have jumped higher if I crouched first. The longer grace period where you can still attempt a stealth take down after being noticed is a nice quality of life change. Increased enemy attentiveness makes stealth more interesting; Now if an enemy sees you, they actually tell their nearby friends and they all come at you, so you can't fish them out one by one as easily, which was the biggest cheese in Lugaru. Higher damage from hitting the ground is satisfying. It was stupid to drop someone from 20 meters high head first only to see them get up and run back to fight you. However I think they went just a bit overboard, especially with the damage you take you if you hit head first. You can literally die from being pushed to the ground and hitting your head in a sand dune. Also football kicking someone in the head when they are down is almost a guaranteed kill, which feels just slightly too powerful, that move being a very easy followup to sweeping someone off their feet. And it works against the player as well. Separating block from crouch was a nice change. Having crouch and block bound in the same key worked in Lugaru's favor, since that way you could duck under a roundhouse kick and block a punch with the same key, and if you spammed block uncontrollably (crouching in front of the enemy), you could be kicked in the head with an unblockable low kick as a punishment. However had the rest of the combat been designed properly, I believe having a dedicated defend key is beneficial, since it's more intuitive than having multiple completely different actions bound to the same key. However as I mentioned, the dodge should be integrated to this new dedicated defend key. The new dodge isn't comparable to the old hanspring anyway, since it doesn't work as a repositioning move. Which it doesn't need to either, since jump is OP. Even if the game actually gets updated to a state resembling a full game, which I don't believe will ever happen, unfortunately I don't believe these fundamental flaws in the design of the combat system will be addressed, and that's why I can't give this game a positive review. It feels like they have forgotten what made Lugaru good and why it worked so well. Maybe they should play that game again, and really ponder it.

Otus’s Owl homeland gets besieged by airborne pirates and Otus, along with his soldier buddy Geddy and a few other trusty friends, must set out to put a stop to their dastardly deeds. Otus’s Owl homeland gets besieged by airborne pirates and Otus, along with his soldier buddy Geddy and a few other trusty friends, must set out to put a stop to their dastardly deeds.  Along the way you’ll team up with rebellious pirate   tand misbehaving spider Twig, using their abilities in conjunction with Geddy’s to foil the plans of those invading pirates. The first thing that will take you aback in this game will most likely be its refined pixel art.  This isn’t pixel art like we saw it back in the Super Nintendo era, nor is it a contemporary mashup of what most developers consider ‘throwback or retro style pixel art.’  This is sophisticated and tastefully crafted pixel art with all the dressings of high resolution graphics. Owlboy’s gameplay is a melange of adventure platforming, aerial navigation and twin stick companion shoot-emup.  With the tap of a button, you can fly freely without any recharge mechanic, as an owl should, and on your own, you may dodge, perform a spin-attack that stuns enemies, and drag select objects around after picking them from the ground. But the meat of the game rests when you pick up your companions.  The game then ventures into the twin stick realm, you’ll be flying with one stick and free arming with the other depending on the abilities of your counterpart.   As such, this is how ability progression plays out in Owlboy - not by purchasing new abilities or unlocking them, but by finding companions and utilizing their skill sets to add to your own. Faults are hard to find in Owlboy, save for some tweaking that needs to be done to make the controls more responsive. It’s just a tad unresponsive, it’s a downfall yet not a catastrophic one.  Like getting an ice cream sundae and finding you didn’t get enough extra chocolate sauce.  No big deal in the end really. The only other notable thing would be that the navigation can be tricky from time to time as you fly around the hub worlds, discover new areas and unlock barricades on past screens with special abilities.  It’s all a little bit hard to keep track off.  But nothing to mare the overall experience. The presentation, story and character arcs are Owlboys strongest weapons.  You’ll find Twigs story arc particurlly poignant and you may find yourself open to the idea of exploring the deep character archetypes that each character is instilled with.  You’ll make friends, you’ll feel the nostalgia from the obvious Zelda influences and may gush a little when the story all comes together.  And it doesn’t hurt that the gameplay is also refreshing, diverse and satisfying.

text: Okay, so... I pretty much knew very little about this game when I picked it up. I was aware that the plot was a big deal and that it was considered to be a good game. I wasn't disappointed. Let me get something out of the way: the story was, indeed, quite amazing. The narrative goes from the main character being a screw up to showing everyone that he was much more than just a kid by the end, and it has an overall feel-good tone all along. The musical score is also brilliant and uplifting (no pun intended, since you fly around as the titular owl boy Otus). The store page didn't lie about the boss fights: each and every one, considering how simple the game mechanics are, feel well balanced and engaging from the very first one. That said, Owlboy feels a bit short for an averagely skilled gamer used to exploration games with puzzles. The main source of longevity for the title is just in going through the story again because otherwise it's all about the collectathon for the 100%. Picture this: every area has some coins, which basically once you reach certain amounts you get health upgrades and QoL upgrades for the guys you use as gunners. The final upgrade in this chain grants you invulnerability (no joke!), which by the time you do get it you'll use it for the otherwise considerably-hard final encounter. If you ignore looking for every collectable and just do the actual game you might clock in at around 5 or so hours; that's not bad, but you can understand where I'm coming from, likely. It should be noted that dying in this game is litterally a minor setback with practically no consequences, given how you are restored to full health and the game likes to auto-save a lot on area transitions and clearing things (such as unlocking a door or collecting some thingamajig). Should you buy it? I guess. It is a good game, after all. The music really is great and the story is memorable. There's a funny moment here and there so it's not too bad. The post-ending extra area that clues you in on some very important key points of the plot also feels well done.
